claims.text: High configurational complexity is the primary governor of enhanced strength and altered deformation or failure behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
High configurational complexity introduces increased local lattice distortion.
High configurational complexity introduces local chemical fluctuations or local elemental ordering.
Lattice distortion and local chemical fluctuations impede dislocation motion.
Lattice distortion and local chemical fluctuations modify defect-nucleation pathways.
Local lattice distortions act as effective dislocation-pinning sites.
Local lattice distortions alter the balance among slip, twinning, and other deformation mechanisms.
Reducing configurational complexity produces fewer lattice distortions.
Alloys with reduced configurational complexity exhibit more conventional dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Under identical testing conditions, the high-complexity alloy will have higher yield strength than the reduced-complexity baseline.
Under identical testing conditions, the high-complexity alloy will have a higher strain-hardening rate than the reduced-complexity baseline.
Under identical testing conditions, the high-complexity alloy will show more pronounced planar slip or twinning than the reduced-complexity baseline.
The hypothesis should apply where plastic deformation is dominated by dislocation dynamics at moderate temperatures and strain rates.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at very high strain rates where additional mechanisms such as cavitation become prevalent.
CrCoNi and related concentrated alloys can display exceptional damage tolerance that improves at cryogenic temperatures.
The quantitative contribution of lattice distortion relative to grain boundaries or short-range order is uncertain.
Processing history may influence the observed mechanical effects.
